key_points.point: The document asserts that AI development is following a rapid, exponential improvement curve, citing benchmarks like the METR Long Tasks graph and others. This trajectory suggests that AI capabilities are scaling predictably and quickly, which accelerationists view as the primary driver for achieving transformative societal benefits. The document notes that while benchmarks have flaws, the consistent trend across diverse tests indicates a clear path forward without immediate signs of a slowdown. This supports the accelerationist goal of building bigger, faster, and stronger AI to solve complex global problems.
key_points.verbatim: This new approach to AI is the outcome of the rapid exponential improvement in AI abilities. That means you can’t understand where we are, and where we might be going, without understanding the increasing capability of AI.

key_points.point: The author highlights the emergence of AI agents capable of autonomous, complex work, framing this as a shift from 'co-intelligence' to 'managing AIs.' This aligns with the accelerationist value of building increasingly powerful systems that can handle significant human workloads. The document argues that this shift is necessary and inevitable, and that organizations must experiment with these new capabilities to remain competitive. It views the rapid development of these agents as a positive, transformative force for work.
key_points.verbatim: Starting in late 2025, we entered a new era thanks to AI agents like Claude Code, OpenAI’s Codex, and OpenClaw. These are AI systems that you can just give work to, sometimes hours of human work, and get back reasonable and useful results in minutes.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section: The Shape of the Thing

key_points.point: The document describes the 'Software Factory' experiment at StrongDM, where AI agents autonomously write, test, and ship production software without human intervention. This demonstrates a practical, experimental approach to AI integration that prioritizes real-world performance over theoretical debates. Accelerationists would view this as a successful test of AI's ability to handle complex, multi-step tasks, proving that radical experimentation is the best way to advance. The author acknowledges that such experimentation is 'likely necessary' for organizations to adapt.
key_points.verbatim: The basic idea of the Factory is that it takes future product roadmaps, written by humans, and turns those into products. Coding agents use those roadmaps to build software while testing agents try out the software in a simulated customer environment.

key_points.point: The author discusses the 'recursive self-improvement' (RSI) loop, where AI systems are increasingly used to build better AI systems. This is framed as an explicit roadmap for major AI companies, suggesting that the exponential curves of capability could steepen further. Accelerationists view this as the ultimate goal of AI development, where progress becomes self-sustaining and accelerates beyond human research capabilities. The document notes that while RSI was once theoretical, it is now an active area of development at major labs.
key_points.verbatim: One reason is that AI companies are telling us, fairly explicitly, what comes next: recursive self-improvement, or RSI. This is the idea that AI systems are increasingly being used to build better AI systems, creating a feedback loop that could accelerate the very curves I showed you above.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI systems exhibit 'jagged' capability profiles, where they excel at structured tasks but fail at common sense or real-world judgment. This unpredictability is a core safety concern because it makes it difficult to certify that an AI is safe for a given job. Safetyists argue that this 'jagged frontier' means we cannot assume general competence, and deploying AI in safety-critical settings without understanding these failure modes is reckless. The document warns that it is dangerous to assume AI is generally competent just because it aces certain tests.
key_points.verbatim: Further, despite these amazing capabilities in tests, companies are still very early in adopting AI, meaning that, as of yet, remarkably little has changed in most organizations. AI remains jagged, capable of some tasks at a high level, while messing up others.

key_points.point: The author describes the 'rolling disruption' of AI, where sudden capability thresholds lead to unpredictable market and societal reactions. This instability is a major safety concern because it outstrips the ability of institutions to govern or adapt. Safetyists would interpret this as a systemic risk, where the pace of development makes it impossible to implement adequate safeguards. The document warns that as the stakes increase, the environment will feel even more unstable.
key_points.verbatim: As AI capability crosses thresholds, it unlocks radical new use cases that change people’s views, sometimes overnight, about what AI can do. At the same time, organizations experimenting with AI will figure out how to make it work for them, leading to sudden announcements about new strategy or large-scale shifts in which kinds of employees companies value most.

key_points.point: The document discusses the potential for recursive self-improvement (RSI) and its uncertain endpoint, noting that major AI labs are actively pursuing this. Safetyists view this as a potential 'phase transition' where AI could become uncontrollable. The author admits that we don't know how far this goes or if AI will hit a ceiling, which safetyists argue necessitates extreme caution and pre-emptive safety measures. The document explicitly links this to the risk of an uncertain endpoint for AI development.
key_points.verbatim: We also don’t know whether LLM-based AIs will eventually hit a ceiling where they cannot get any better, or where the jagged frontier never smooths out. I don’t think we know anything for certain, but I also think we are past the point where recursive self-improvement is science fiction.

key_points.point: The author emphasizes that while we can see the 'shape of the Thing,' we still have the opportunity to influence it, but the window of time to do so is closing. This aligns with the safetyist goal of proactive governance and alignment work before capabilities reach a point of no return. The document notes that current governance is lacking, which is a critical safety failure. It argues that we must act now to set precedents for how AI is used in work, schools, and government.
key_points.verbatim: We clearly don’t have rules or role models for how AI gets used at work, in schools, or in government. That’s a problem, but it also means that every organization figuring out a good way to use AI right now is setting a precedent for everyone else.

key_points.point: The document notes that despite impressive test scores, AI adoption in most organizations is still in its infancy, meaning remarkably little has changed for the average worker. Skeptics use this to argue against the hype surrounding AI's immediate impact on the economy. The document cautions that we should not assume AI's capabilities in tests translate directly to widespread, reliable real-world performance. This supports the skeptic view that we should focus on the actual, measurable impact of AI rather than speculative future scenarios.
key_points.verbatim: Further, despite these amazing capabilities in tests, companies are still very early in adopting AI, meaning that, as of yet, remarkably little has changed in most organizations.

key_points.point: The author discusses how AI was used as a convenient excuse for large-scale layoffs at the financial services company Block, even if the role of AI was likely exaggerated. Skeptics point to this as evidence that companies use AI hype to justify cost-cutting and labor displacement. The document highlights the danger of AI being used as a cover for corporate decisions that negatively impact workers. This supports the skeptic argument that we must hold companies accountable for the real-world harms they cause today.
key_points.verbatim: On February 26, financial services company Block announced 40% layoffs, implying this was due to AI. It is likely that the role of AI was greatly exaggerated, and AI was merely used as cover for large-scale layoffs.

key_points.point: The document notes that the conflict between the Pentagon and Anthropic over AI control is complex and still not fully understood. Skeptics would argue that this conflict illustrates the dangerous entanglement of AI companies with military and government interests, which should be subject to public scrutiny. The author's observation that these cases are often not what they appear to be supports the skeptic's call for transparency and accountability in AI governance.
key_points.verbatim: And then, to cap off the week, on February 27 a very public conflict occurred between the Pentagon and AI company Anthropic over who should be able to control the rules for how Claude could be used by the government. In a lot of ways, each of those cases were not what they first appeared to be.

key_points.point: The author acknowledges that history is full of technologies that were expected to change everything overnight but instead took decades to reshape the economy. Skeptics use this historical perspective to counter the 'AI will change everything fast' narrative. The document suggests that while AI is powerful, it may follow a more gradual path of integration, which supports the skeptic's call for evidence-based policy rather than panic-driven regulation.
key_points.verbatim: History is full of technologies that were supposed to change everything overnight but instead took decades to fully reshape the economy.

factual_claims.claim: The best AI models score 94% on the Google-Proof Q&A benchmark, compared to 30-70% for graduate students.
The latest AI models reach or exceed parity with top-performing human experts on complex tasks 82% of the time on the GDPval benchmark.
